beats.narration_text: Hi, I am Adwait Changan, and this video is about why citations do not make an AI answer true. Today we are going to learn the difference between an agent finding a document and an agent actually using it. Those are two different events, and only one of them can be checked automatically.

props.command: If the answer cites a source, is it grounded?
output: A citation needs three checks. Two of them a machine can do.
The third is whether the quote supports the claim, and that is judgement.
An answer can cite a real source, quote it verbatim, and still be false.

beats.narration_text: A citation has to survive three checks before it means anything. Does the source actually exist. Does the quoted text appear in it, word for word. And does that quote actually support the claim being made. The first two are string comparisons. The third is a judgement about meaning, and no amount of engineering turns it into one.

props.caption: The first two are free. The third is the only one that decides whether the answer is true.

beats.narration_text: And notice what retrieval alone gives you. It hands back a document that scored well against the question. That is a relevance signal, not a truth signal. Retrieval answers did anything look related. Grounding answers does this specific sentence follow from that specific passage. Most systems ship the first and call it the second.

beats.narration_text: And here is the checker, honestly labelled. Twelve lines. Source missing. Quote not in source. Otherwise, the citation checks out. Read the docstring, because it says what the function does not do. It never attempts to decide whether the quote supports the claim, and pretending otherwise would be the actual bug.

props.title: grounding.py — check()
props.code:
def check(claim: str, source: str, quote: str) -> str:
    """Two of the three checks a citation needs. The third is not in here.

    Machine-checkable: the source exists, and the quote appears in it verbatim.
    NOT machine-checkable: whether the quote actually supports the claim. That is a
    judgement about meaning, and nothing in this function attempts it.
    """
    if source not in CORPUS:
        return "MISSING_SOURCE"
    if quote not in CORPUS[source]:
        return "QUOTE_NOT_IN_SOURCE"
    return "CITATION_CHECKS_OUT"
props.sparkLine: It says what it cannot do.

beats.narration_text: So be precise about what a citation buys you. It proves the source exists. It proves the text was not invented. It does not prove the quote is relevant, it does not prove the claim follows from it, and it absolutely does not prove the answer is true. Four of those six are things people assume they got for free.

props.sparkLine: What it proves. What it does not.

Does NOT prove: the quote is relevant
Does NOT prove: the claim follows from it
Does NOT prove: the numbers were read correctly
Does NOT prove: the answer is true
props.caption: A citation is evidence that something was read. Not evidence that it was understood.

beats.narration_text: Which gives three things worth building, in order of how much they buy you. Check the source exists, because it is nearly free. Check the quote is verbatim, because that catches invented text. And then put the quote next to the claim where a human can see both at once, because that is the only check that catches the fourteen against thirty.

beats.narration_text: Which reframes what a citation is for. It is not there to convince the reader. It is there to let the reader disagree quickly. If your interface shows a source link that nobody can open beside the sentence it supports, you have built decoration.

beats.narration_text: So, the verdict. Retrieval finds what looks related. That is a relevance signal, not a truth signal, and shipping the first as the second is the most common mistake in this whole area. A citation survives three checks: the source exists, the quote is verbatim, and the quote supports the claim. Only the first two can be automated. In four test answers, two citations passed every automatic check and one of those two was still false, because a real document was quoted word for word to support a number it does not say. Build for the third check. It is the only one that decides whether the answer is true.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here is the prompt. Take three answers my system produced with citations attached. For each one, quote the exact sentence from the source that supports it, then tell me whether that sentence actually says what the answer claims, or only something nearby. Flag every case where the citation is real but the claim goes further than the quote. Run that against your own output. The phrase to watch for is goes further than the quote, because that is the failure that survives every automatic check you will ever write.
